title: Channelopathies that cause patterning defects link developmental biology and neuroscience

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Channelopathies that cause patterning defects link developmental biology and neuroscience

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The deep symmetry between developmental biology and neuroscience is shown by the many ion-channel diseases (channelopathies) that produce patterning defects, and by the applicability of neuroscience tools, from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols, to morphogenetic decisions.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2025, The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine › Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Thinking Beyond the Brain

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It can be seen in numerous channelopathies that result in patterning defects (see Table 1 in [110], and [111, 112, 113]), and in the applicability of the tools of neuroscience—from drugs to optogenetics to training protocols—to morphogenetic decisions.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Multiscale Wisdom of the Body: Collective Intelligence as a Tractable Interface for Next-Generation Biomedicine”, BioEssays : news and reviews in molecular, cellular and developmental biology (2025), doi:10.1002/bies.202400196; section “Bioelectricity as the Interface to Multicellularity › Thinking Beyond the Brain”. Scope: Vertebrates including humans; ion channel genes and developmental phenotypes

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2025-wisdom-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large public genotype-phenotype resources make the channelopathy component highly analysable. The broader symmetry and applicability of all neuroscience tool classes are only partly covered and not uniquely established by shared ion-channel mechanisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Systematically estimate enrichment of developmental-patterning phenotypes among pathogenic ion-channel variants and catalogue controlled morphogenetic effects of drugs, optogenetic perturbations and training protocols. Enrichment and reproducible control across modalities support the empirical generalization.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Phenotype annotation and ascertainment vary by gene.

Deep symmetry is interpretive rather than a single endpoint.

Training-protocol evidence is much thinner than channelopathy evidence.

fields.value:
data existence: 0.9

data adequacy: 0.7

operationalizability: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The channelopathy half can be tested now with standard enrichment methods on public gene, variant, and phenotype resources. Ascertainment bias and the breadth of malformation terms keep that test from being clean, and it says nothing about optogenetics or training protocols applied to morphogenesis. The symmetry claim is therefore only partly resolvable from data that exist today.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take the IUPHAR ion-channel gene set and test whether Human Phenotype Ontology and ClinVar annotations for structural malformations are enriched relative to frequency-matched non-channel genes. Enrichment would support the channelopathy-patterning clause; no enrichment would refute it. Applicability of drugs, optogenetics, and training to morphogenesis is a separate experimental question those databases do not contain.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Human clinical terms only partly cover the vertebrate developmental scope.

The databases do not record whether neuroscience tools alter morphogenetic decisions.

Channel genes are heavily sequenced, so phenotype enrichment can be an ascertainment artifact.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Among human disease genes in the Human Phenotype Ontology annotations, numerous ion-channel genes cause both structural patterning defects (craniofacial or limb malformation) and nervous-system phenotypes, and ion-channel disease genes carry patterning phenotypes more often than non-channel disease genes with the same depth of phenotype annotation.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: fetch.py downloads the four files. analysis.py defines ion-channel genes as those with a non-NOT GOA molecular-function annotation to GO:0005216 or a descendant (553 genes, 209 of them HPO disease genes), keeps HPO annotations under HP:0000118 Phenotypic abnormality for 5,269 genes, and propagates each gene's terms up the is_a hierarchy. It counts channel genes annotated to both a face/limb patterning branch and HP:0000707, then compares the fraction of channel vs non-channel genes with a patterning annotation by Fisher's exact test and by a Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio with a one-sided Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel z test over ten equal-sized strata of genes ranked by number of distinct phenotype terms.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: (a) at least 20 ion-channel genes (GO:0005216 ion channel activity or a descendant, any evidence, human GOA) are annotated in HPO genes_to_phenotype to both a patterning term (HP:0001999 Abnormal facial shape, HP:0000202 Orofacial cleft, HP:0001159 Syndactyly, HP:0010442 Polydactyly or HP:0009815 Aplasia/hypoplasia of the extremities, or any descendant) and a nervous-system term (HP:0000707 Abnormality of the nervous system or descendant); and (b) among all HPO-annotated genes, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio for carrying a patterning term, ion-channel vs non-channel genes, stratified by deciles of each gene's number of distinct HPO terms, is > 1.2 with one-sided Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel p < 0.05.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: fewer than 10 ion-channel genes meet (a); or the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio is < 0.8 with p < 0.05 for depletion and fewer than 20 genes meet (a). Any other outcome (e.g. >= 20 such genes but no depth-adjusted enrichment, or enrichment with 10-19 genes) is pre-registered as 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: ion-channel disease genes with both a face/limb patterning phenotype and a nervous-system phenotype in HPO

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: depth-stratified Mantel-Haenszel OR = 0.591, one-sided CMH p(enrichment) = 0.998

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Only the first clause is tested: 'numerous channelopathies that result in patterning defects'. 'Channelopathy' is a human disease gene (any HPO annotation) whose product has GO ion channel activity (GO:0005216, any evidence code, NOT-qualified lines removed). 'Patterning defect' is mapped to five HPO structural-malformation branches of the face and limbs, chosen because they are the craniofacial and limb patterning outcomes Levin's cited examples emphasise; brain malformations are deliberately excluded because they are also nervous-system phenotypes and would make the overlap circular. 'Numerous' is fixed at >= 20 genes. The link to neuroscience is operationalized as co-annotation with a nervous-system phenotype, and the 'deep symmetry' as enrichment of patterning phenotypes in channel genes relative to other disease genes after controlling for how heavily each gene is phenotyped (HPO term count deciles), since syndromic genes accumulate many terms. The second clause (neuroscience tools such as drugs, optogenetics and training applied to morphogenesis) is not in these databases and is not tested.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Human Phenotype Ontology gene-to-phenotype annotations (genes_to_phenotype.txt), release accompanying hp/releases/2026-09-01

Human Phenotype Ontology (hp.obo)

Gene Ontology, basic edition (go-basic.obo)

GOA human GO annotations (GAF), via the GO Consortium

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The literal claim holds: 59 of 209 ion-channel disease genes (28%) have a face or limb malformation in HPO, and every one of them also has a nervous-system phenotype (e.g. KCNJ2, the Andersen-Tawil gene; CACNA1C, Timothy syndrome; KCNH1, Temple-Baraitser and Zimmermann-Laband; KCNK9, Birk-Barel; NALCN; PIEZO2; TRPV4). That is well above the pre-registered 'numerous' threshold of 20.

The specific link does not hold: channel genes carry patterning phenotypes less often than other disease genes (28% vs 34%; 32% vs 41% among genes with nervous-system phenotypes), and after stratifying by annotation depth the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio is 0.59 (one-sided CMH p = 0.002 for depletion). Patterning defects are a common feature of syndromic disease genes in general, so their presence among channelopathies is not by itself evidence of a special developmental role for ion channels. By the pre-registered rule this combination (>= 20 genes but depletion) is 'mixed', not 'supports'.

GO:0005216 with any evidence code is broad: it includes intracellular channels and some genes whose channel function is peripheral (e.g. SEC61A1, BNIP1, TMCO1, OCA2). A stricter plasma-membrane channel set could shift the odds ratio either way.

The patterning set is five face/limb malformation branches chosen in advance; 'Abnormal facial shape' contributes most genes (45) and includes mild dysmorphic features, which are common in neurodevelopmental syndromes and may be secondary to brain or muscle defects rather than primary patterning errors.

HPO reflects what clinicians record; dysmorphology is ascertained more often in syndromic, pediatric conditions than in the adult-onset arrhythmias, myotonias and epilepsies typical of channelopathies. Depth stratification addresses annotation volume, not this case-mix difference.

Human only; the claim's scope is vertebrates. The second clause (neuroscience tools applied to morphogenesis) is not tested. HPO and GOA are 'current' releases fetched at run time, so exact numbers will drift; the SHA-256 values identify the files used.
